title: Peripheral Nerve and Root Compression: Cranial Neuropathies, Entrapments, Radiculopathy, and Neuropathic Pain
subject: Nervous System (NEUR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers injury to cranial nerves, spinal roots, and peripheral nerves from compression, inflammation, and trauma: Bell palsy, trigeminal neuralgia, carpal and cubital tunnel syndromes, thoracic outlet syndrome, disc herniation, radiculopathy, sciatica, lower limb entrapments, spinal stenosis, complex regional pain syndrome, and phantom limb pain. Nearly every question here is an anatomy problem. The stem gives a pattern of numbness, weakness, and reflex change, and you must decide whether the lesion lies in the cord, a root, a plexus trunk, or a single nerve, and at what level. The mechanism of compression (ischemia, demyelination, then axon loss) explains the order in which symptoms appear and why some recover quickly and others do not.
prerequisites: Dermatomes, myotomes, and the segmental levels of the major stretch reflexes
Brachial and lumbosacral plexus organization and the course of the median, ulnar, tibial, and common fibular nerves
Course and branches of the facial and trigeminal nerves
Myelin, saltatory conduction, and Wallerian degeneration
Upper versus lower motor neuron signs

connections.how: A central disc or stenosis that compresses the cord or cauda equina produces the cord and cauda equina syndromes taught there, rather than a single radiculopathy.
A pontine plaque at the trigeminal root entry zone causes trigeminal neuralgia in a young adult.
Hypothyroidism, diabetes, acromegaly, pregnancy, and beta-2 microglobulin amyloid in long-term dialysis add volume to the carpal tunnel or make nerves more vulnerable to pressure.
HSV reactivation, VZV (Ramsay Hunt syndrome), and Lyme disease are infectious causes of lower motor neuron facial palsy.
Disc degeneration, facet and uncovertebral osteophytes, and ligamentum flavum thickening are the structural causes of root entrapment and stenosis.

terms.def: Focal nerve injury where a nerve passes through a tight anatomical space, caused by pressure, ischemia, and traction.
Dysfunction of a spinal nerve root producing dermatomal pain or sensory change, myotomal weakness, and reduced reflexes.
The area of skin supplied by the sensory fibers of a single spinal root.
The group of muscles innervated by the motor fibers of a single spinal root.
Conduction block from focal demyelination with intact axons, which recovers as myelin is repaired.
Axon disruption with preserved connective tissue sheaths, followed by Wallerian degeneration and slow regrowth along the original path.
Abnormal electrical crosstalk between adjacent demyelinated axons, so activity in one fiber excites its neighbor.
Leg pain, numbness, or weakness brought on by standing or walking and relieved by flexion, caused by lumbar canal narrowing.
Spinal cord dysfunction, producing upper motor neuron signs and tract sensory loss below the level of the lesion.
Pain evoked by a stimulus that is normally not painful, such as light touch.
Abnormal sensitivity to ordinary sound, here from paralysis of the stapedius muscle.

sections.title: Bell palsy: lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy

blocks.text: The facial nerve (CN VII) leaves the pons, crosses the cerebellopontine angle with CN VIII, and enters the internal acoustic meatus. It then runs through the facial canal in the temporal bone, a long bony tunnel whose narrowest part is the labyrinthine segment near the geniculate ganglion, and exits at the stylomastoid foramen to supply the muscles of facial expression. Along the way it gives off branches for tearing, sound damping, and taste.

blocks.title: Facial nerve path and the branches given off in the canal
steps: CN VII leaves the pons and enters the internal acoustic meatus
Geniculate ganglion: greater petrosal nerve to the lacrimal gland
Nerve to stapedius: damps loud sound
Chorda tympani: taste, anterior two-thirds of tongue; submandibular secretion
Stylomastoid foramen: motor branches to facial muscles
blocks.caption: A lesion loses every function whose branch leaves at or distal to the lesion, so the extra deficits localize the level.

blocks.text: Bell palsy is an acute, unilateral, lower motor neuron facial palsy with no other identified cause. The leading explanation is inflammation of the nerve, most often linked to reactivation of latent herpes simplex virus in the geniculate ganglion. The inflamed nerve swells inside the rigid canal, which compresses its own blood supply, so ischemia and demyelination follow. Diabetes, pregnancy (especially late pregnancy and the early postpartum period), and Lyme disease are associated risks; Lyme disease is a classic cause of bilateral facial palsy. Weakness develops over hours to about 3 days, often with ear pain.

Because the nerve itself is damaged, the entire half of the face is weak: the forehead cannot wrinkle, the eye cannot close, and the mouth droops. On attempted closure the eye rolls upward (Bell phenomenon), and the blink of the corneal reflex is lost on that side although the afferent limb (V1) is intact. A stroke behaves differently. The part of the facial nucleus that supplies the forehead receives corticobulbar input from both hemispheres, so an upper motor neuron lesion weakens only the contralateral lower face.

blocks.title: Localizing a facial palsy
rows: Whole half of face weak, forehead included
Final common pathway to all facial muscles damaged
Lower motor neuron lesion (nucleus or nerve)
Bilateral cortical input to upper face nucleus
Lesion proximal to the nerve to stapedius
Loss of taste, anterior two-thirds of tongue
Lesion proximal to the chorda tympani
Lesion at or proximal to the geniculate ganglion
Vesicles in ear canal, ear pain
VZV reactivation in the geniculate ganglion
Ramsay Hunt syndrome, not Bell palsy
blocks.caption: A lesion at the stylomastoid foramen causes facial weakness alone; lesions higher in the canal add the branch deficits.

blocks.text: Most patients recover over weeks to months because the usual injury is demyelination with intact axons. When axons degenerate, regrowth can be misdirected: fibers meant for one muscle reach another (synkinesis, such as eye closure with smiling), and salivary fibers can reach the lacrimal gland, causing tearing while eating. Incomplete eye closure with reduced tearing exposes the cornea to drying and ulceration.

blocks.predict: A patient cannot raise the right eyebrow or close the right eye, and loud sounds are uncomfortable in the right ear, but tearing is normal. Where is the lesion?
blocks.explain: The whole right face is weak, so this is a lower motor neuron lesion. Hyperacusis places it proximal to the nerve to stapedius, and normal tearing places it distal to the geniculate ganglion, in the facial canal between the two.
blocks.check: The facial nerve flow and the localization table.

sections.title: Carpal tunnel syndrome: median nerve compression at the wrist

blocks.text: The carpal tunnel is a rigid channel with the carpal bones forming its floor and walls and the flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament) forming its roof. Through it pass the median nerve and nine flexor tendons: four of flexor digitorum superficialis, four of flexor digitorum profundus, and flexor pollicis longus. Because the walls cannot stretch, anything that adds volume to the contents raises pressure on the nerve, which is the most compressible structure in the tunnel.

blocks.title: From added volume to axon loss
steps: Added volume or swelling within the rigid tunnel
Pressure rises on the median nerve
Venous congestion and ischemia of the nerve's small vessels
Focal demyelination slows conduction across the wrist
Intermittent paresthesia, worse at night
Sustained pressure causes axon loss: numbness, thenar atrophy
blocks.caption: Early symptoms are reversible because they reflect ischemia and demyelination; constant numbness and atrophy mean axons have been lost.

blocks.title: Risk factors and how each raises tunnel pressure
rows: Glycation and microangiopathy make the nerve less tolerant of pressure
Tendon sheath thickening and repeated pressure peaks
blocks.caption: Every listed risk either adds volume to a fixed space or lowers the nerve's tolerance of pressure.

blocks.text: Distal to the retinaculum the median nerve supplies sensation to the palmar thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of the ring finger. Its recurrent (motor) branch supplies the thenar muscles abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, and the superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis, and digital branches supply the lateral two lumbricals. The result is paresthesia in that finger distribution and, later, weak thumb abduction and opposition with flattening of the thenar eminence.

Symptoms are typically worse at night because the wrist often rests in flexion during sleep, which raises tunnel pressure, and patients wake and shake the hand to relieve them. Tinel sign is paresthesia produced by tapping over the nerve at the wrist, where demyelinated segments are mechanosensitive. Phalen sign is paresthesia produced by holding the wrist fully flexed for about a minute. Nerve conduction studies show prolonged median sensory and motor latencies across the wrist.

Sensation over the thenar eminence and central palm is spared because the palmar cutaneous branch leaves the median nerve proximal to the wrist and runs superficial to the retinaculum. This is a key distinction: numbness of the palm itself places a median nerve lesion in the forearm or above, not in the carpal tunnel.

Each intervertebral disc has two parts. The annulus fibrosus is a ring of concentric fibrocartilage lamellae rich in type I collagen, whose fibers alternate in direction to resist twisting. The nucleus pulposus is a central gel, a remnant of the notochord, made of water-binding proteoglycans (mainly aggrecan) in a type II collagen network, which spreads compressive load to the annulus. The adult disc is largely avascular and depends on diffusion from the vertebral end plates.

With age, proteoglycan content and water fall, the nucleus loses turgor, and the annulus develops fissures under repeated flexion and axial load. Herniation occurs when nucleus material pushes through a torn annulus. It is most common in the lumbar spine at L4 to L5 and L5 to S1, the levels that bear the most load and motion. The posterior longitudinal ligament is strong centrally but narrow in the lumbar region, leaving the posterolateral annulus unsupported, so most herniations are posterolateral.

Pain has two sources. The outer annulus is innervated (by the sinuvertebral nerve), so annular tears cause axial back pain. Displaced nucleus material compresses the root mechanically and, because it is normally sequestered from the immune system, provokes an inflammatory reaction around the root; this chemical radiculitis explains why pain can be severe with a small herniation and why many herniations shrink and improve as macrophages resorb them.

Which root is hit depends on how roots exit. In the lumbar spine each root exits through the foramen below the pedicle of its own vertebra, and that root leaves high in the foramen, above the disc. The next root down crosses the back of the disc in the lateral recess on its way to exit one level lower. A posterolateral L4 to L5 herniation therefore compresses the traversing L5 root, and an L5 to S1 herniation compresses S1. A far lateral (foraminal) herniation is the exception and compresses the exiting root (L4 at L4 to L5). A large central herniation can compress several roots of the cauda equina.
In the cervical spine, roots C1 to C7 exit above the vertebra of the same number and C8 exits between C7 and T1, so a C5 to C6 herniation compresses C6 and a C6 to C7 herniation compresses C7.

blocks.title: Predicting the root from the disc level
blocks.text: MRI shows a posterolateral herniation at L4 to L5. The L4 root exits through the L4 to L5 foramen above the disc, so it is usually spared. The L5 root is traveling down in the lateral recess across the back of this disc, so it is compressed. Expect L5 findings: pain and numbness over the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot, weak great toe extension and ankle dorsiflexion, and no change in the knee or ankle reflex. If the same disc herniated far laterally into the foramen, it would compress L4 instead, with a reduced knee reflex.

A spinal root is formed from a dorsal (sensory) and ventral (motor) rootlet bundle that join near the intervertebral foramen; the dorsal root ganglion, containing the sensory cell bodies, usually lies within the foramen. Roots are vulnerable because they have thinner connective tissue sheaths than peripheral nerves and run through bony openings that narrow with degeneration. In younger adults the usual cause of entrapment is a herniated disc. In older adults it is spondylosis: osteophytes from the uncovertebral and facet joints, disc height loss, and ligament thickening narrow the foramen.

Root compression produces a predictable triad in the distribution of that single root: sharp, radiating pain and paresthesia in the dermatome, weakness in the myotome, and a reduced or absent reflex if the root carries one. Signs are lower motor neuron signs, because the injury is to the axons of the final motor pathway. Weakness is usually partial, because most muscles receive fibers from two or more roots. Maneuvers that narrow the foramen worsen the pain: in the neck, extension with rotation and axial loading toward the affected side (Spurling test); in the low back, coughing or straining, which raise epidural venous and cerebrospinal fluid pressure.

blocks.title: Root lesions to predict
rows: Elbow extension, wrist flexion, finger extension
Anterior knee, medial leg to medial malleolus
Lateral leg, dorsum of foot, great toe
Great toe extension, dorsiflexion, inversion, hip abduction
Posterior calf, lateral foot and sole, little toe
blocks.caption: Dermatomes overlap, so sensory loss is often smaller than the full dermatome; reflex and motor changes are more localizing.

blocks.text: Electrodiagnosis confirms the level by mechanism. Because most root compression lies proximal to the dorsal root ganglion, it cuts the central process of the sensory neuron but leaves the cell body and its peripheral axon intact. Sensory nerve action potentials recorded from the limb therefore remain normal despite numbness, whereas a plexus or peripheral nerve lesion reduces them. Denervation of the paraspinal muscles, supplied by the posterior rami that branch just beyond the root, also points to a root rather than a plexus.

blocks.predict: A patient has numbness of the thumb and index finger with a reduced biceps reflex, yet the median and radial sensory nerve action potentials are normal. Root or peripheral nerve?
blocks.explain: Root (C6). The lesion is proximal to the dorsal root ganglion, so the peripheral sensory axons stay connected to their cell bodies and conduct normally even though signals no longer reach the cord.
blocks.check: The paragraph on electrodiagnosis and the root table.

sections.title: Sciatica and the straight leg raise

blocks.text: The sciatic nerve forms from the L4 to S3 roots, leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen usually below piriformis, and descends in the posterior thigh before dividing into the tibial and common fibular nerves. Sciatica is radicular pain in this territory: pain that radiates from the buttock down the posterior or posterolateral thigh and below the knee, often with paresthesia in the foot. In most cases the cause is compression of the L5 or S1 root by a lumbar disc herniation.

blocks.title: From L5 to S1 disc herniation to sciatica
steps: Degeneration and load tear the posterolateral annulus
Nucleus pulposus herniates posterolaterally at L5 to S1
Traversing S1 root compressed and inflamed
Ectopic firing in the damaged root
Pain radiates buttock to posterior leg, below the knee
Weak plantarflexion, lateral foot numbness, reduced ankle reflex
blocks.caption: The pain is felt in the root's territory, not at the site of compression, because ectopic impulses are read by the brain as coming from the root's normal receptive field.

blocks.text: Radiation below the knee is the key feature. Pain from facet joints, the sacroiliac joint, or muscle is referred somatic pain, which is usually deep, poorly localized, and stays above the knee. Radicular pain follows a dermatome into the leg and foot and is often sharper and shooting.

The straight leg raise test exploits root mobility. With the patient supine and the knee straight, the examiner flexes the hip. This pulls the sciatic nerve and draws the L5 and S1 roots a few millimeters through their foramina. A normal root slides freely, but an inflamed root tethered over a herniation is stretched, reproducing the radiating pain. The test is positive when pain below the knee appears between about 30 and 70 degrees of hip flexion; below 30 degrees the root barely moves, and beyond 70 degrees hamstring and lumbar joint strain cause nonspecific discomfort. Dorsiflexing the foot at the point of pain adds tension and increases it. The test is sensitive for L5 or S1 root irritation but not specific. Pain in the affected leg when the opposite leg is raised (crossed straight leg raise) is less sensitive but much more specific for herniation. Upper lumbar roots (L2 to L4), which form the femoral nerve, are tested instead by hip extension with the patient prone.

Not all sciatic pain is radicular. Compression of the sciatic nerve by piriformis in the buttock, pelvic masses, or trauma can mimic it, but these spare the paraspinal muscles and produce findings in a nerve rather than root pattern. Sciatica with saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, or bilateral weakness suggests cauda equina compression, covered in NE-20-H.

The thoracic outlet is the passage from the root of the neck to the axilla. The brachial plexus trunks and the subclavian artery pass through the interscalene triangle, bounded by anterior scalene in front, middle scalene behind, and the first rib below. The subclavian vein passes in front of anterior scalene, then through the costoclavicular space between the clavicle and first rib. Distally, the neurovascular bundle runs beneath pectoralis minor. Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) is compression of these structures at any of these sites.

The lower trunk, formed by C8 and T1, lies lowest in the plexus and rests directly on the first rib, so it is the part most often compressed. The usual culprits are a cervical rib (an elongated costal element of C7) or the fibrous band that extends from it to the first rib, scalene muscle hypertrophy or anomalous insertion, and post-traumatic scarring. Raising the arm overhead narrows the costoclavicular space and tightens the structures over the rib, so symptoms are characteristically worse with overhead activity.

blocks.title: Forms of thoracic outlet syndrome
rows: Chronic compression and traction of the lowest trunk
Paresthesia of medial forearm, ring and little fingers; weak, wasted intrinsic hand muscles
Repeated compression causes stenosis, post-stenotic dilation, thrombus, and distal emboli
Arm pallor, coolness, fatigue with use, reduced pulse; digital ischemia
Repeated compression injures the vein wall and causes thrombosis, often after strenuous overhead effort
Arm swelling, cyanosis, heaviness, distended superficial chest and shoulder veins
blocks.caption: Neurogenic symptoms follow C8 and T1, so they resemble ulnar nerve disease; vascular forms add color, temperature, or swelling changes.

blocks.text: Neurogenic TOS produces paresthesia and aching along the ulnar side of the hand and the medial forearm (the C8 and T1 dermatomes) and weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles, which are T1 dominant. Because the median nerve also carries C8 and T1 fibers to the thenar muscles, thenar wasting can be prominent even though sensory symptoms are ulnar sided.

Two distinctions matter on exams. First, ulnar neuropathy at the elbow does not cause medial forearm numbness, because the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve arises from the medial cord, above the elbow; medial forearm sensory loss therefore points to the lower trunk or the C8 and T1 roots. Second, an apical lung (Pancoast) tumor can invade the same lower trunk, and it adds a Horner syndrome from involvement of the sympathetic chain, along with weight loss or a smoking history. A lower trunk traction injury from forced arm abduction (Klumpke palsy) produces a similar distribution acutely.

The trigeminal nerve (CN V) carries general sensation from the face, cornea, oral cavity, and anterior scalp through its ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2), and mandibular (V3) divisions, and V3 also carries motor fibers to the muscles of mastication. Its sensory root enters the lateral pons. Near the brainstem there is a short segment where myelin changes from central (oligodendrocyte) to peripheral (Schwann cell), and this root entry zone is mechanically and metabolically vulnerable.

Trigeminal neuralgia is paroxysmal, unilateral, electric shock or stabbing pain lasting from a fraction of a second to about 2 minutes, in one or more divisions, most often V2 and V3 and rarely V1 alone. Attacks are triggered by innocuous stimulation of trigger zones around the lips, nose, or cheek: light touch, chewing, talking, shaving, brushing teeth, or a breeze. Between attacks the patient is usually pain free, and a brief refractory period may follow an attack. In the classic form the sensory examination is normal. It is most common after age 50 and more common in women.

blocks.title: From vascular compression to triggered pain
steps: Artery loop (often superior cerebellar) pulses against the root entry zone
Focal demyelination of trigeminal root axons
Ectopic impulses arise at the demyelinated segment
Ephaptic crosstalk from touch fibers to nociceptive fibers
Afterdischarges amplify into a burst
Light touch or chewing triggers a paroxysm of pain
blocks.caption: Demyelinated axons become hyperexcitable and electrically coupled, so ordinary touch input recruits pain fibers.

blocks.text: The usual cause is compression of the root near the pons by a blood vessel, most often a loop of the superior cerebellar artery. Chronic pulsation demyelinates the root, and large touch fibers (A-beta) can then excite nociceptive fibers, so a light touch sets off a burst of pain. A short silent period follows while the hyperexcitable membrane recovers. The paroxysms respond to drugs that produce use-dependent blockade of voltage-gated Na+ channels, which supports the idea that repetitive ectopic firing drives the attacks.

In a younger adult, especially with bilateral symptoms, consider multiple sclerosis: a demyelinating plaque at the trigeminal root entry zone in the pons produces the same mechanism without a vessel. Other secondary causes include cerebellopontine angle tumors such as meningioma, epidermoid tumor, or vestibular schwannoma. Persistent sensory loss, an absent corneal reflex, weakness of chewing, or constant background pain all suggest a structural lesion rather than classic neuralgia. Postherpetic neuralgia differs because it follows a zoster rash, most often in V1, and causes continuous burning pain with allodynia rather than brief shocks.

sections.title: Cubital tunnel, tarsal tunnel, and common fibular nerve entrapment

blocks.text: These three entrapments follow the same rules as carpal tunnel syndrome: a nerve passes a fixed bony or fibrous point, and pressure, traction, or both cause ischemia, demyelination, and eventually axon loss in the territory distal to that point.

blocks.title: Three entrapments compared
rows: Ulnar nerve behind medial epicondyle, under fibrous arch of flexor carpi ulnaris
Tibial nerve under flexor retinaculum behind medial malleolus
Common fibular nerve winding around fibular neck
Leaning on elbow, prolonged elbow flexion, arthritis, old fractures
Ganglion, varicose veins, flat foot, ankle trauma, tenosynovitis
Leg crossing, squatting, tight cast, fibular fracture, weight loss
Little finger and ulnar half of ring finger, palmar and dorsal
Sole (medial and lateral plantar nerves), burning, worse standing
Lateral leg and dorsum of foot
Interossei, hypothenar muscles, adductor pollicis, medial lumbricals
Dorsiflexion and toe extension (foot drop), eversion
Ankle movement; heel if calcaneal branch arises above tunnel
blocks.caption: The spared functions are as diagnostic as the deficits, because they show which branches leave above the compression.

blocks.text: The ulnar nerve is stretched by elbow flexion and the tunnel beneath the flexor carpi ulnaris arch narrows, so symptoms worsen with the elbow bent, as when holding a phone or sleeping with arms flexed. Weak interossei cause difficulty spreading and closing the fingers, and weak adductor pollicis makes the patient flex the thumb tip with flexor pollicis longus (median nerve) to grip paper (Froment sign). Clawing of the ring and little fingers is milder with an elbow lesion than with a wrist lesion, because a lesion at the elbow also weakens the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus, removing the pull that flexes the fingertips. Numbness of the dorsal ulnar hand places the lesion above the wrist, because the dorsal cutaneous branch leaves in the forearm and bypasses the Guyon canal.

The common fibular nerve lies just under the skin against bone at the fibular neck. Its deep branch supplies the ankle and toe dorsiflexors, and its superficial branch supplies fibularis longus and brevis (evertors) and the lateral leg skin. Injury causes foot drop with a high-stepping gait to clear the toes.

In tarsal tunnel syndrome the tibial nerve is compressed beneath the flexor retinaculum behind the medial malleolus, where it divides into the medial and lateral plantar nerves. The result is burning paresthesia of the sole that worsens with standing and walking, while ankle strength and the ankle reflex are preserved because the calf muscles are supplied above the tunnel.

blocks.title: Fibular neuropathy or L5 radiculopathy?
blocks.text: Both cause foot drop and numbness over the dorsum of the foot, because the L5 root supplies the dorsiflexors through the fibular nerve. Test inversion. Tibialis posterior inverts the foot; it is innervated by the tibial nerve but carries L5 fibers. In a fibular neuropathy at the knee, inversion is normal because the tibial nerve is untouched. In L5 radiculopathy, inversion is weak, and hip abduction (gluteus medius, superior gluteal nerve, L5) may also be weak. Back pain radiating below the knee and a positive straight leg raise further favor the root. Paraspinal denervation on electromyography confirms it.

Spinal stenosis is narrowing of the central canal, lateral recesses, or foramina. In older adults it is acquired: disc height loss with posterior bulging, facet joint hypertrophy and osteophytes, thickening and infolding of the ligamentum flavum, and degenerative spondylolisthesis all crowd the canal. Congenitally short pedicles, as in achondroplasia, lower the threshold. What is compressed depends on the level. In the lumbar spine the canal contains the cauda equina, so stenosis affects multiple roots. In the cervical spine it contains the cord, so stenosis causes myelopathy.

blocks.title: Mechanism of neurogenic claudication
steps: Standing or walking extends the lumbar spine
Ligamentum flavum buckles inward; canal and foramina narrow
Epidural pressure rises; venous outflow from the roots is impaired
Walking raises the metabolic demand of crowded roots
Root ischemia: leg pain, numbness, heaviness
Sitting or bending forward widens the canal; symptoms ease
blocks.caption: Posture changes canal size, so lumbar flexion relieves symptoms and extension provokes them.

blocks.text: Neurogenic claudication is bilateral or unilateral buttock and leg pain, numbness, or weakness brought on by standing or walking and relieved within minutes by sitting or leaning forward. Patients walk farther pushing a shopping cart or going uphill, and they tolerate cycling, all of which flex the spine. The examination at rest is often near normal, because compression is positional. Vascular claudication must be distinguished (table).

blocks.title: Neurogenic versus vascular claudication
rows: Muscle ischemia from fixed arterial narrowing
Standing as well as walking; downhill worse
Walking or exercise only; uphill worse
Reduced pulses, cool, hairless, shiny skin
blocks.caption: Relief by standing still points to arterial disease; relief only by flexion points to the spine.

blocks.text: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy is the most common cause of spinal cord dysfunction in older adults. The cord is squeezed between disc and osteophyte in front and a buckled ligamentum flavum behind, especially in extension, and repeated motion adds ischemic injury. Compression of the lateral corticospinal tracts gives upper motor neuron signs below the level: spastic, stiff gait, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign, and a positive Hoffmann sign. Dorsal column involvement causes poor proprioception, unsteady gait, and clumsy hands. Roots at the compressed level may add lower motor neuron signs, such as a reduced biceps reflex with brisk reflexes below. Neck flexion may send an electric sensation down the spine (Lhermitte sign), and bladder symptoms appear late. Sensory findings separate it from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

blocks.predict: A 70-year-old has leg pain after walking two blocks that eases when he leans on a shopping cart, with normal foot pulses. Why does leaning forward help?
blocks.explain: Lumbar flexion stretches the ligamentum flavum flat and opens the canal and foramina, lowering epidural pressure and restoring venous drainage and blood flow to the cauda equina roots. Normal pulses argue against arterial claudication.
blocks.check: The neurogenic claudication flow and comparison table.

sections.title: Complex regional pain syndrome and phantom limb pain

blocks.text: Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) is continuing pain in a limb after an injury, out of proportion in severity and duration to the original event and not confined to one nerve or dermatome. It most often follows a fracture (distal radius fracture is a classic setting), surgery, a sprain, or immobilization. Type I, formerly called reflex sympathetic dystrophy, occurs without an identifiable nerve injury. Type II, formerly called causalgia, follows a documented injury to a nerve. Diagnosis is clinical, using the Budapest criteria, which require symptoms and signs across the categories below with no better explanation.

blocks.title: Features of CRPS and their mechanisms
rows: Peripheral and central sensitization of pain pathways
Temperature asymmetry, red or blue skin
Altered sympathetic vasomotor control and neurogenic vasodilation
Weakness, stiffness, tremor; changes in hair, nails, skin; patchy bone loss
Disuse, altered cortical motor control, and trophic effects of inflammation
blocks.caption: No single test confirms CRPS; the pattern of findings across categories makes the diagnosis.

blocks.text: Several mechanisms combine. Injured nociceptor terminals release substance P and calcitonin gene-related peptide, causing vasodilation, plasma leakage, and swelling (exaggerated neurogenic inflammation) along with local cytokines. Repeated nociceptive input sensitizes dorsal horn neurons (central sensitization), so touch becomes painful. After injury, nociceptors can express adrenergic receptors, coupling sympathetic activity to pain. Early disease often shows a warm, red limb, and later disease more often a cool, blue one. The limb's representation in the somatosensory cortex shrinks and distorts. Imaging may show patchy periarticular osteopenia and increased uptake on bone scan.

Phantom limb pain is pain perceived in a limb that has been amputated, often burning, cramping, or shooting. It must be distinguished from phantom sensation, the nonpainful feeling that the limb is still present, which most amputees experience, and from residual limb (stump) pain, which arises in the remaining tissue, for example from a neuroma. Mechanisms operate at three levels. Cut axons form neuromas that fire spontaneously, and dorsal root ganglion neurons become hyperexcitable. In the dorsal horn, loss of normal input and central sensitization amplify signals. In the cortex, neighboring regions expand into the deafferented area; after arm amputation the face area may invade the hand area, so touching the face can evoke sensation in the phantom hand, and greater remapping is associated with more pain. Severe pain before amputation increases the risk.

integration.text: Anatomy decides the localization in every condition in this chapter. Where a branch leaves relative to the compression explains spared palm sensation in carpal tunnel syndrome, preserved tearing in a distal facial palsy, preserved inversion in fibular neuropathy, and medial forearm numbness in thoracic outlet syndrome. The level of the dorsal root ganglion explains why root lesions spare sensory nerve action potentials. The developmental origin of a cervical rib and the course of the roots relative to the discs explain who is compressed and where.

Pathology and physiology explain the time course. Pressure first impairs microvascular flow and myelin, which is reversible, and only later destroys axons, which recover slowly and sometimes with misdirected regrowth. Endocrine disease, pregnancy, dialysis amyloid, and rheumatoid synovitis act by adding volume to fixed spaces; HSV, VZV, and Borrelia act by inflaming nerves in bony canals; multiple sclerosis acts by demyelinating a vulnerable root entry zone. Chronic pain syndromes show the limit of a purely structural view: in CRPS and phantom limb pain the nervous system itself becomes the generator, through peripheral sensitization, central sensitization, and cortical reorganization.

summary: Bell palsy is a lower motor neuron CN VII palsy that weakens the whole half of the face (upper motor neuron lesions spare the forehead); reduced tearing, hyperacusis, and lost anterior tongue taste localize the lesion along the canal.
Carpal tunnel syndrome is median nerve compression under the flexor retinaculum, with nocturnal paresthesia of the thumb to the lateral ring finger, thenar weakness, and spared palm sensation.
Posterolateral lumbar herniation compresses the traversing lower root (L4 to L5 disc affects L5); cervical roots exit above their vertebra (C5 to C6 disc affects C6).

Radiculopathy gives dermatomal pain, myotomal weakness, and reflex loss with lower motor neuron signs; sensory nerve action potentials stay normal because the lesion is proximal to the dorsal root ganglion.
Sciatica is radicular pain below the knee, usually from L5 or S1; the straight leg raise stretches these roots and is sensitive, while the crossed test is specific.
Thoracic outlet syndrome compresses the C8 to T1 lower trunk, subclavian artery, or vein, worse with the arm overhead; medial forearm numbness separates it from ulnar neuropathy at the elbow.
Trigeminal neuralgia is brief, triggered V2 or V3 pain from vascular demyelination of the root entry zone; in young or bilateral cases, suspect multiple sclerosis.
Fibular neuropathy causes foot drop with preserved inversion; L5 radiculopathy weakens inversion and hip abduction as well.
Lumbar stenosis causes neurogenic claudication relieved by flexion with normal pulses; cervical stenosis causes myelopathy with upper motor neuron signs below the level.

CRPS is limb pain out of proportion to an injury with sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor, and trophic changes (type II after nerve injury); phantom limb pain reflects neuroma firing, central sensitization, and cortical remapping.
